title: The Relation of the Word to God and Participants
english: the murmur. We are being instructed by this from the beatitudes; for does not the poor in spirit possess the other virtues? The poor in spirit is also a fellow-sufferer; and because of this he mourns; for if he were without sympathy, he would not be poor in spirit. He has meekness; for if he were angry, he could not be called blessed. He has righteousness.

Regarding the one with much power and the more stable condition, the so-called ones are marveled at. Concerning [the phrase]: 'they saw many in the holy city'; yet Jerusalem was not holy, 'she who killed the prophets' (Hebrews 11:37), which the Savior left behind saying: 'Behold, your house is being left to you' (Matthew 22:7). Those who walk upon the earth and have their citizenship in the heavens (Philippians 3:20) were seen in the holy city, the city of the living God.

Concerning [the word]: 'they were seen';—these thicker perceptions are grasped by the fat ones. He has thirty-three, three, eleven, and thirty-three. They become fifteen. Often the number fifteen has been said to be raised to the two testaments; for it teaches the seven and the eight; for it has been said to us in the additions that it is also a triangle and, having been handed over as a pentad, it has a relationship to the sensible things; for how was it not destined, since a change of face has occurred?

Concerning [the phrase]: 'if we say that he remained there';—not immediately. In another stay occurring there. This is almost at the beginning of the kingdoms, but concerning the end, that is, when they finished the rest for war against Saul. Concerning [the phrase]: 'did he not first release and depart?';—by no means, examine the ascents toward the word. Since I say to you also that which is about Abraham: 'He had two sons, one from the slave-girl and one from the free woman' (Genesis 21:2). And he, not being Abraham, had them. Through Hagar he had Ishmael as Abram, but Abraham had this.

And now that: 'it corresponds to the present Jerusalem'. I do not say 'now' in order that you might take the correspondence according to a symbol. But the correspondence is said in many ways. Immediately, even in grammar, the aspirated ones are said to correspond to the unaspirated, and the long to the short. But among those who deal with logic, the opposites are said to correspond. You divide the animal into rational and irrational, and into mortal and immortal, and into having a head and being headless. The rational and the mortal is not corresponding...

not, but the irrational. The correspondence here according to the apostle to the preceding thing is symbolic. In order that I might say it more thickly: there is a sensible sacrifice and circumcision, and both are spiritual. It is not necessary to take the circumcision according to the flesh as corresponding to the spiritual sacrifice, and the more bodily sacrifice not to the spiritual circumcision, but merely a sacrifice.

Furthermore: 'By the word of the Lord the heavens were established' (Ps 33:6), and again: 'For straight is the word of the Lord' (Isa 55:11)?—the same things, when they are not sensible, seem by thought to be one thing and another. One is the Holy Spirit, and we say of him various gifts. If you look toward the gifts, it seems to be a multitude of holy spirits. You have, indeed: 'and the spirit of prophets is subject to the prophets' (1 Cor 12:10). It is also said, the spirit of Elijah and the spirit of Elisha. These are not different things in essence, but by thought and by the relation of the partakers, they are said in the plural, 'spirits'.

And the Word, therefore, the Word of God, when he was still with God—for 'the Word was with God' (Jn 1:1)—has no relation to any other, but to God alone, and secondly also to his partakers: for 'those' [he called] 'gods, those to whom the Word of God became' (Ps 82:6). The Word of God was with him. Therefore, his Word is without relation to God, but it became in a relational way toward the partakers of it.

The partakers do not participate in one single imposition, as was said concerning the Spirit: for one has a word of wisdom, another a word of knowledge; for not one and another is this same Word according to the underlying reality. There are some having knowledge of spiritual things, knowledge of the truth, of the dogmas of piety; for they are not able to explain something about them. And we have known thinking men to be very understanding, yet unable to speak even by chance. These have a word of knowledge. But when he has the having of knowledge and the ability to explain and to teach and to carry the thoughts in it to others, it is a word of wisdom. For Wisdom herself says, without fail: 'she examines words', clearly in a teaching manner. The same Word, therefore, becomes toward the prophets, and is toward God, and toward those becoming gods from his union. And
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Blessing in All Seasons
english: We do not seek the same kind of relationship; for indeed, toward the Father it is unsurpassed. The communion toward God is not by condescension, but toward those who have become gods according to their merit, power, and the proportion of their progress. And toward the prophets it happens thus: 'the Word who came into being with Jeremiah' (Jeremiah 1:5). He did not say 'the Being,' but 'the one coming into being.' And coming into being happens according to that measure. And here, therefore, we have explained differently the direct Word of God, whose works are in faith. We have said that the teaching-word is able to be.

Furthermore: what kind of spirit shall we receive? —By an intention, the mouth of God shall receive a spirit instead of: when through the word it leads into the knowledge of those things which it judges to be acceptable. 'Remove the crookedness from your mouth.' 'And his mouth calls upon the bold death.' When the spirit is toward God and toward the Son, it is not called 'spirit of the mouth,' but when it is ministered to those able to receive it by the word. Furthermore: do you not say someone is a participant of righteousness being practical? —The one having righteousness with understanding and being able to make it clear to another just as he himself possesses it. Furthermore: do you not say he does this by the word? —I do not say by the word in the spoken sense.

2 'I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise is continually in my mouth' (Psalm 34:1). He who blesses God at all times is the one who is giving thanks in all things falling upon him. And the apostle also writes: 'giving thanks in all things' (1 Thessalonians 5:18). He who gives thanks to God does not do so only for pleasant things; he does this, but also for unpleasant things. Job, indeed, does not bless God only in prosperity and the salvation of children and the other surrounding wealth, but also when all was taken from him at once. When indeed all his ordered things, the existing things, were taken from him, he gives thanks to God, and 'he did not sin,' he says, 'Job did not act foolishly toward the Lord, nor did he give unfaithfulness to God' (Job 1:21-22). He who speaks concerning providence saying: 'he ought to have done thus or thus,' imputes foolishness to God and [speaks of] how much he did not consider God regarding what He ought to have done. When indeed someone says: 'it was necessary for the old to die before the young, the parents before the children, and the healthy not to die, but the sick,' he gives foolishness to the [Divine]...

Being cared for and provided for. Thus, 'he did not give foolishness to God' (cf. Ps 34:1). ... 'Blessed is the Lord' (Ps 34:1). Since therefore both times and seasons are different, and it is fitting to give thanks in everything, he rightly says: 'I will bless the Lord at all times' (Ps 34:1). There is no time when I do not bless the Lord. Even if the things coming upon me are unpleasant, I receive them as good.

Another word said: 'Whatever comes to you from the Lord, receive it as good.' You would not say, seeing one who is sick and being treated by a skilled physician, that he is thankful to the physician desiring salvation; for when [the physician treats him], even if he divides him with a sword so that he may be saved, he accepts it, not only when the physician gives him pleasant helps. He looks not to the pleasant or the unpleasant of the things coming, but to the profitable and the effective. Therefore every time is a time to bless God. We take the time in two ways: the necessary season and the condition of the one helping.

We say, for example, regarding the healthy, that the time of a skilled [physician] is midday and the time of dinner is evening; but regarding the one suffering, we do not take the time as a season, but rather looking to how his body is. In both ways the saint blesses God 'at all times' (Ps 34:1); for he knows that it is by providence, and that he who provides knows even better what will be effective for him. 'Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, in everything give thanks' (1 Thess 5:16-18). If the saint rejoices always, he is never submerged or cast down when grim things are present; for even at these things he rejoices, he rejoices as if at athletic contests. He who follows the victory sees the contests and expects the crowns and the prizes, and rejoices, even if the surrounding circumstances are unpleasant.

Therefore, 'I will bless' (Ps 34:1). And so that no one thinks the blessing happens by spoken word, such as someone saying by a promise: 'His praise is in my mouth continually' (Ps 63:3). In praising him, I bless him. 'His praise is in my mouth continually' (Ps 63:3). But we do not say this so that something impossible might follow, that the praise is in the spoken word continually. But this is impossible; for while sleeping one does not do this, while eating at times one does not do this; but thus it must be praised: all that I do, even if I eat and drink and sleep, I undergo these things thanking God. Thus also it should be heard from: 'Always...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Praise and the Meek
english: “Rejoice.” If you receive this by grace through operation, the one sleeping does not have this; by power he has it. “Pray without ceasing.” If you take this as praying in a demonstrative manner, it cannot be performed without ceasing. For indeed, if one is recorded historically, it is said that one prays “three times of the day,” at noon or around the ninth hour; let us grant also the evening. Therefore, to pray without ceasing is such a thing: there is no other prayer or petition for good things from God.

Whenever anyone, through all [time], does what he does, he asks God for good things, he prays. Even if he does not do his own [specific prayer], having desire to encounter the profitable things, he prays. The desire itself is prayer; for he has the desire. Whatever he may do, even if he is hindered from doing his own prayer, he has the asking of God. Thus also it is said in the Wisdom of Sirach: “Instruct the pious in wisdom through all [time]” (Sirach 24:23). How can one instruct wisdom through all [time]? If we take it this way—and such things are often taken this way by custom—as when we often seek something and desire to learn where we might encounter it; they say: “He always sits at this physician's office and is continuously there,” not taking the whole day, but rather, when he sits, he sits there. He did not therefore simply say “through all [time] is the praise,” but “of Him”; for he who thinks to praise without right thoughts, without the truly theological [thoughts], does not praise Him, does not praise Him.

“My soul shall be praised in the Lord” (Psalm 34:1). My soul is not praised upon anything else previously than upon participating in God; for just as another seeks to be praised upon a skill, or upon knowledge, or upon a dignity or honor, so the saint wants his soul to be praised in the Lord. He knew no other praise of the soul except this; for even if, as I have said, someone is praised upon knowledge, this praise, being compared to another occurring upon God, is not praise at all. We say often: “Nothing is as sweet as honey.” There are indeed other sweet things, but they are not sweet as compared to honey. And in another psalm he says: “From you is my praise in a great assembly” (Psalm 22:5). Which [praise], which He gives to me, is praise not occurring upon anything else...

Or upon you. 'My soul shall praise in the Lord.' 'In you,' he says, 'we shall praise all the day.' The whole time of our life is called a day. And 'in you' may mean 'upon you' or 'by you.' Both run toward the holy one. And upon you God is praised, and by God one receives the wine. 3 Listen, O meek, and be glad. Just as the foolish man wants to hide what he says and does when he is not known, so the diligent, reclining with God, wants what he says and does to be known by all. He wants his light to shine before men, so that they, seeing, might glorify God. He wants his words to go to others; for it has been said, 'talk in your perambulations' (Acts 8:31). He who talks to others talks, not to himself previously. Since therefore I have set before myself to praise the Lord at all times and to have his praise continually in my mouth, so that my soul may be praised in him, 'listen, O meek, and be glad' (Psalm 34:8). Imitate me, and you also become such. But if he calls the meek greater than himself, he says, 'listen, O meek,' because I, being educated toward you and having established you, am such; for the lesser exists and belongs to the greater. The disciples are praiseworthy and praising the Lord—much more the teachers, having established them. Therefore take it either way: that the greater than me, the meek, having heard, were glad because they had such a disciple or companion.

4 Magnify the Lord with me. Having spoken about the meek to them, he turns the word further: 'and upon me magnify the Lord with me.' For someone magnifies God not by adding greatness to him from something small, but when he is able to take in his greatness. For the sun, rising, is not viewed as being of its actual size. Rather, it is seen as slightly greater; for it does not himself receive an increase, but the one viewing is improved, seeing him more clearly. 'Magnify God,' think great things about God, 'with me'; for 'magnify God' means to think great things about him. 4 And we shall exalt his name above the same. He—
